PREPARED BY MS.A.KIRUTHIKA , AP/CSE, KEC

Lean Software Development

Foundational principles, the seven wastes, and the core Lean tools — a complete, examination-ready study reference illustrated throughout with a single running example: the College Attendance Management System (CAMS).

Origin Toyota Production System, adapted by Tom & Mary Poppendieck Category Agile mindset, not a fixed framework Running Example College Attendance Management System (CAMS)
Origins Lean Thinking Defined Seven Values Waste & Flow Seven Wastes Amplify Learning Decide Late Deliver Fast Empower Team Build Integrity In See the Whole Lean Tools Value Stream Mapping Five Whys WIP Area Charts Pull Systems How Concepts Connect Case Study: CAMS Lean Dashboard Glossary Revision Tables
Running example used throughout College Attendance Management System (CAMS) — faculty mark attendance, students check their attendance percentage, and students below the eligibility threshold are alerted automatically. Every Lean concept below is grounded in this one system.
1FOUNDATIONS

Origins and Nature of Lean

  • Lean is a management philosophy that traces back to the Toyota Production System (TPS), developed in Japanese manufacturing during the mid-twentieth century to eliminate waste and maximize customer value on the factory floor.
  • The word "lean" described this manufacturing discipline for decades before it crossed into software.
  • In the first decade of the twenty-first century, Tom and Mary Poppendieck adapted the underlying ideas of lean manufacturing to Agile software development.
  • When capitalized as Lean, the term refers specifically to this adaptation — the application of lean thinking to the practice of building software.

Lean Is a Mindset, Not a Framework

A common misunderstanding is to treat Lean as another process framework alongside Scrum or XP. The three differ in kind:

ApproachWhat It Provides
ScrumA defined framework of roles (Scrum Master, Product Owner, Team), events (Sprint, Daily Scrum, Review, Retrospective), and artifacts (Backlog, Increment).
XP (Extreme Programming)A collection of concrete engineering practices — pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, and similar techniques.
LeanNeither roles nor a fixed set of practices. Lean is primarily a mindset — "Lean Thinking" — that can be layered on top of Scrum, XP, Kanban, or any other delivery approach.
Working Definition Lean is a mindset focused on eliminating waste and creating maximum value for the customer.
Applying the Idea — CAMS
  • Adopting Scrum gives the team sprints and a backlog.
  • Adopting XP gives it testing discipline.
  • Adopting Lean gives the team a lens — a habit of continually asking which activities genuinely help a student see accurate attendance data sooner, and which activities merely consume effort without moving that outcome forward.
The same lens applies outside software: a student who spends two hours searching for tangential information, writes twenty pages when five were required, waits two days for a signature, and repeatedly switches between unrelated assignments has invested substantial effort — but a large share of it produced no value toward the actual goal. Lean asks one repeatable question of any process: "Which activities actually create value, and which activities are waste?"
2FOUNDATIONS

Lean Thinking Defined

Formal Definition Lean thinking is a business methodology intended to organize human activities so that they deliver more benefit to society, create value for individuals, and eliminate waste.
Compact Definition "Becoming lean is a process of eliminating waste with the goal of creating value."

Restated operationally: Lean thinking means doing more of the work that is valuable, doing less of the work that is not, and continuously refining how the remaining work gets done.

Three Foundational Terms

Value

Anything that satisfies a genuine customer need.

In CAMS, value is created the moment a student can trust the attendance percentage on their screen, or a faculty member marks a class in under a minute.

Waste

Any activity that consumes effort without contributing to that value.

An unused CAMS analytics report generated weekly but never opened is waste, regardless of how much engineering effort it required.

Lean Thinking

The mindset of continuously maximizing value while minimizing waste, applied at every stage of the development lifecycle — not as a one-time exercise.

3FOUNDATIONS

The Seven Lean Values

Lean Software Development is organized around seven values. Together they form the operating principles of Lean Thinking.

#ValueMeaningRef.
01Eliminate WasteRemove any activity that does not contribute value to the customer.§4–5
02Amplify LearningUse feedback from each iteration to improve how the software is built.§6
03Decide as Late as PossibleCommit to irreversible decisions only once sufficient information exists.§7
04Deliver as Fast as PossibleShorten cycle time so customer value arrives sooner.§8
05Empower the TeamTrust people closest to the work with the authority to decide how it gets done.§9
06Build Integrity InBuild quality into the product continuously rather than inspecting it in at the end.§10
07See the WholeOptimize the entire value stream, not any single stage in isolation.§11
4ELIMINATING WASTE

Waste and Flow

Of the seven Lean values, Eliminate Waste is treated first because it underlies the rest: most other Lean practices exist to expose or remove waste in one form or another.

Definition Waste is anything that does not contribute value to the customer. If an activity does not help satisfy — or delight — the customer's needs, it may be considered waste, regardless of how much effort it consumed.

Because waste and delay are linked this way, the corollary follows directly: removing waste speeds up value creation. This is why waste elimination is treated as the entry point into Lean practice rather than an isolated housekeeping task.

Applying the Idea — CAMS If the CAMS team spends three days waiting for database access before a developer can even begin coding the "view attendance percentage" screen, that waiting time adds directly to how long students wait for the feature — without a single line of code being written any faster.
5ELIMINATING WASTE

The Seven Wastes of Software Development

Lean manufacturing originally catalogued seven categories of waste on the factory floor; the Poppendiecks mapped each onto software development. A convenient memory aid is the acronym formed from their initials: P E E T W M D.

5.1 Partially Done Work

5.2 Extra Processes

5.3 Extra Features

5.4 Task Switching

5.5 Waiting

5.6 Motion

5.7 Defects

5.1 Partially Done Work

  • Work started but not fully finished, tested, and deployable represents value that has not yet reached the customer.
  • Lean emphasizes delivering work that is genuinely "done done" — complete, tested, integrated, and deployable — because incomplete work cannot be used no matter how much effort has gone into it.
CAMS Example Suppose 80% of the "low-attendance alert" feature is coded, but automated testing is incomplete and it has not been integrated with the notification service. A student at risk of falling below the minimum attendance requirement still receives no alert. Ninety percent of a working feature is, from the student's perspective, the same as no feature at all — much like a restaurant that prepares 90% of a meal but never serves it.
Key PointPartially done work creates an inventory of unfinished effort and delays the moment value is actually delivered.

5.2 Extra Processes

  • Activities performed beyond what is actually required — processing that does not move the product closer to the customer.
  • A frequently cited example: excessive time-tracking and status reporting that nobody downstream reads or acts on.
CAMS Example A developer spends several hours each week compiling a detailed activity report for a stakeholder who never opens it. The developer is undeniably working, but the activity does not improve the attendance system in any way.
Important Distinction Not all documentation is waste. Documentation required for compliance, safety, maintenance, or communication between teams can create real value. The Lean question is not "is this documentation?" but "Does this activity provide value relative to the effort it consumes?"

5.3 Extra Features

  • Functionality built beyond what customers actually requested or need.
CAMS Example The department asks for student login, attendance marking, and percentage reporting. The team additionally implements animated attendance charts, a five-color theming engine, and an experimental elective-recommendation module — none of which was requested.
  • Extra features often arise for an understandable reason: a developer is excited about new technology and wants an opportunity to use it. Learning that technology may hold future value, but the feature itself, if unrequested, does not serve the current customer.
Governing PrincipleBuild what provides value, not simply what is technically interesting.

5.4 Task Switching

  • Also called context switching — unnecessary movement between different tasks, projects, or processes.
CAMS Example A developer alternates every twenty minutes between coding the attendance dashboard, fixing a bug in the leave-request module, answering a support ticket, and writing documentation. Each switch requires reconstructing context before real progress resumes.
Task Switching
→
Loss of Focus
→
Additional Cognitive Effort
→
Delay
Key PointSustained focus on one unit of work at a time reduces the waste caused by task switching.

5.5 Waiting

  • Occurs whenever people or work items sit idle pending something they require to continue — specification approval, system access, a license, a code review, another team's output, infrastructure, or technical support.
CAMS Example A developer completes the "attendance report export" feature, but deployment requires the head of department's sign-off. That approval takes two days. During those two days, no additional value reaches any student or faculty member — the time is pure waiting.
ConceptWaiting time contributes directly to overall lead time and cycle time without adding any value in return.

5.6 Motion

  • Unnecessary physical or coordination movement associated with the work process — most visibly, team members walking to another location simply to have a conversation because they do not sit or work together.
CAMS Example A front-end developer repeatedly walks across the building to consult the back-end developer about the attendance API's response format, rather than the two working from a shared, documented contract. Each walk is small, but repeated many times, the accumulated delay is significant.
  • More broadly, motion can be understood as any inefficient movement of people or information between stages or locations — not limited to walking.

5.7 Defects

  • Errors or bugs that require additional effort to discover, correct, retest, and sometimes support after release.
CAMS Example A developer introduces a rounding error in the attendance-percentage calculation. If a unit test catches it immediately, the fix is small and contained. If it reaches production undetected: a student reports incorrect attendance → support investigates → a developer reproduces the issue → fixes it → the fix is tested → the fix is deployed. The later a defect surfaces, the greater the rework required.
Key PointPractices such as Test-Driven Development (TDD) prevent many defects before they enter the codebase, reinforcing the broader Lean principle that quality should be built into the development process rather than relying solely on late defect detection.

The Seven Wastes — Quick Reference

WasteCAMS Illustration
Partially Done WorkAn 80%-complete alert feature that cannot yet notify any student
Extra ProcessesA weekly status report nobody reads
Extra FeaturesAn unrequested elective-recommendation engine
Task SwitchingA developer rotating across four unrelated modules every 20 minutes

6THE REMAINING SIX VALUES

Amplify Learning

  • Software development is a knowledge-intensive process. Requirements, architecture, and testing strategy are rarely fully understood at the outset; they are progressively discovered as the team builds, observes, and adjusts.
Definition Amplify learning means using feedback generated by the project to continuously improve how the software is being built — deepening the team's understanding of customer needs, viable architectural solutions, and effective testing strategies.
Build
→
Get Feedback
→
Learn
→
Improve
→
Build Again
CAMS Example The team initially assumes faculty want five configurable dashboard layouts for marking attendance. After releasing an early version to a pilot group, the team learns that almost everyone prefers a single, simple, one-tap attendance-marking screen. Incorporating that feedback into the next iteration is amplifying learning in practice.
NoteIn Lean, every iteration is treated as an opportunity to learn something that can improve the iteration that follows — not merely as a checkpoint for reporting progress.
7THE REMAINING SIX VALUES

Decide as Late as Possible

Definition Make important decisions when sufficient information is available — ideally at the last responsible moment — rather than committing early under uncertainty.
  • This principle does not mean "avoid making decisions." It means avoiding premature commitment when the cost of being wrong is high and better information is likely to arrive soon.
  • Early decisions made under incomplete information are more prone to error; delaying a decision until more evidence exists reduces that risk, provided the delay itself does not become a new source of waste.
CAMS Example Should attendance percentages be computed in real time on every screen load, or pre-calculated on a nightly batch schedule? Rather than committing immediately, the team builds small prototypes of both approaches and measures actual load under realistic conditions before locking in the architecture — because reversing this decision after full-scale development begins would be costly.
Key IdeaDelay irreversible decisions, not all decisions. Routine, low-cost, reversible decisions can and should be made quickly.
8THE REMAINING SIX VALUES

Deliver as Fast as Possible

Definition Lean places strong emphasis on reducing cycle time — the time between receiving a request for a feature and delivering that feature to the customer.
  • Speed matters because a feature under development creates no value for the customer until it is delivered.
Shorter Cycle Time
→
Faster Delivery
→
Earlier Customer Value
→
Faster Feedback
→
Faster Learning
CAMS Example A department requests: "Add SMS alerts for students below 75% attendance." Bundled into a six-month release with unrelated modules, students wait six months. Shipped as a small, independently deliverable unit in three weeks, at-risk students begin receiving warnings — and a chance to correct their attendance — far sooner.
Note — Cost of Delay Every day a valuable feature is not delivered represents lost opportunity — for CAMS, this might mean more students crossing the attendance shortfall threshold before they are ever warned. Minimizing cost of delay, using pull systems and queues (§16), is a direct application of this Lean value.
9THE REMAINING SIX VALUES

Empower the Team

Definition Create a focused, effective work environment in which people are trusted and directly involved in the decisions that shape their work — reflecting Lean's broader commitment to respect for people.
  • Rather than management deciding every detail and simply assigning tasks, team members are given appropriate responsibility for deciding how the work itself gets done.
  • The Poppendiecks draw this from three principles from the Toyota Product Development System:

1. Entrepreneurial Leadership

Leadership that encourages initiative and ownership rather than issuing detailed instructions.

2. Expert Technical Workforce

Skilled technical staff are trusted to apply their own expertise to how a problem is solved.

3. Responsibility-Based Planning & Control

Teams take direct responsibility for planning and controlling their own work.

Directive approach

"Implement the attendance-alert feature exactly this way, using this specific library, in this exact sequence."

Lean-oriented approach

The product owner states the outcome — "students below 75% attendance should be alerted before it affects their exam eligibility" — and the CAMS team determines the most suitable technical approach.
Key PointEmpowered teams make decisions closer to the actual work, which typically means those decisions are made with more accurate, current information than decisions made further away from the work.
10THE REMAINING SIX VALUES

Build Integrity In

Definition Build software that makes intuitive sense to users, satisfies their needs, and forms a coherent whole — with a coherent architecture that is usable, fit for purpose, maintainable, adaptable, and extensible.
  • The central idea: quality should be built in early, rather than added at the end through a final round of testing and defect-fixing.
CAMS Example Suppose the team waits until the final week before an academic term to test the entire system. It then discovers, all at once: attendance percentages calculated incorrectly for students with mid-semester course changes, a security gap in faculty login, and a confusing marking interface. Fixing all of this under deadline pressure is expensive and risky. Testing continuously, module by module, would have surfaced each issue while it was still small and cheap to fix.
NoteWhen a defect is discovered early, Lean thinking calls for stopping the ongoing work and fixing it immediately, rather than letting it travel further through the system where it becomes more expensive to correct. Summarized as: build quality in — don't inspect quality in later.
11THE REMAINING SIX VALUES

See the Whole

Definition Examine the entire value stream from end to end, rather than optimizing a single activity in isolation. A value stream is the complete sequence of activities through which work moves from an initial request to delivered value.
Requirement
→
Design
→
Coding
→
Testing
→
Deployment
→
Customer

11.1 Local Optimization vs. System Optimization

  • A frequent source of waste is improving one stage of a process without regard for the stages around it.
  • If the requirements stage becomes very fast but coding remains slow, requirements simply pile up faster than coding can absorb them — the queue in front of coding grows, and total time from request to delivery does not improve.
CAMS Example Consider a CAMS onboarding pipeline: Registration → ID Verification → Attendance Account Activation → Approval. If registration is made twice as fast but approval is still handled manually, once a week, by a single administrator, a student's overall wait to have a working attendance account may not improve at all — the bottleneck has simply moved earlier in the queue.
Key PrincipleOptimize the entire system end to end, not isolated activities within it. This connects directly to Value Stream Mapping (§13), the primary Lean tool for seeing — and improving — the whole.
12LEAN TOOLS & TECHNIQUES

Overview of Lean Tools

Lean values describe what a team should aim for; Lean tools give the team concrete ways to observe waste and act on it. The core tool set includes:

Just-in-Time

Produce or deliver only what is needed, when it is needed — avoiding excess inventory of unfinished or unused work.

Kaizen

Continuous, incremental improvement carried out by the people doing the work, rather than large infrequent overhauls.

Queuing Theory

The mathematical study of waiting lines, used to understand and reduce bottlenecks in a workflow.

Leadership

Leadership that supports empowered, responsibility-based teams rather than command-and-control management.

Cost of Delay

A way of quantifying the economic impact of not delivering a feature sooner.

Value Stream Mapping

A visual technique for tracing a unit of value's actual journey and exposing where waste occurs.

The remainder of this section examines the tools most directly used to identify and reduce waste in day-to-day practice: Value Stream Mapping, Five Whys, the WIP Area Chart, and Pull Systems — each demonstrated using CAMS.

13LEAN TOOLS & TECHNIQUES

Value Stream Mapping

Definition
Purpose
Key Elements
MMF
Mapping Steps
Processing Time
Waiting Time
Lead Time
Waste ID
Bottleneck ID
CAMS Example
Interpretation

1Definition

A Value Stream Map (VSM) is a visual representation of the steps through which a unit of value moves from inception to delivery. As the Poppendiecks describe it, it is essentially a simple pencil-and-paper exercise — a technique that originated in manufacturing — used to find waste in any process, including a software team's workflow.

2Purpose

  • To find where time is being spent across the full journey of a feature.
  • To identify waste — especially time spent waiting rather than working.
  • To answer the key Lean question: not "can developers code faster?" but "why is the work waiting between stages, and what would remove that wait?"

3Key Elements of a Value Stream Map

  • Boxes — each box represents one processing step the feature passed through (e.g. Requirements, Design, Coding).
  • Arrows — connect the boxes in the exact order the work actually moved, since a VSM documents real history, not a hypothetical plan.
  • A work / wait divider line — time spent actively working is plotted above the line, and time spent waiting is plotted below the line, exactly as drawn in the reference diagram, making the split between the two instantly visible.
  • Timestamps at every stage, recording both the processing time and the waiting time.

4MMF — Minimal Marketable Feature

An MMF (Minimal Marketable Feature) is the smallest possible chunk of the product that customers are willing to prioritize — often taking the form of a user story, requirement, or feature request. A VSM should always start with a small unit of value like this, ideally one the team has already built and delivered, so that the map reflects real history rather than a guess.

5Steps in Building a Value Stream Map

  1. Start with a small unit of value. Choose something the team has already delivered — ideally the smallest possible unit, an MMF.
  2. Trace its complete journey. Reconstruct every step the feature passed through, from inception to delivery.
  3. Draw each step as a box, and connect the boxes with arrows in the order the work actually moved.
  4. Record both processing time and waiting time at every step, because it is the accumulated waiting time — not the coding time — that usually accounts for most of the delay.

Because a VSM traces the actual history of a real, already-delivered feature, the resulting diagram is a straight line — there are no decision branches, since it documents what genuinely happened rather than what might happen.

6Processing Time, Waiting Time & Lead Time

  • Processing Time (also called Active Work) — the time the team is genuinely working on the feature at a given stage.
  • Waiting Time — the time the feature sits idle at a stage, blocked on something else (approval, review, access, another team).
  • Lead Time — the total elapsed time from the moment work starts to the moment the feature is delivered.
Lead Time  =  Processing Time  +  Waiting Time

7Waste Identification

  • The map makes waiting time visible in a way a task list or status report normally does not.
  • Any stage whose waiting time is large relative to its processing time is flagged as a likely source of the Lean waste "Waiting" (§5.5) and, if the feature sits unfinished across several such stages, also "Partially Done Work" (§5.1).

8Bottleneck Identification

  • The stage with the largest waiting time is the strongest candidate for the process bottleneck — the point where work accumulates and the overall lead time is most inflated.
  • Per the Lean value See the Whole (§11), fixing this one stage benefits the entire value stream far more than speeding up a stage that already flows well.

9CAMS Example — "Low-Attendance Alert" Feature

The CAMS team traces the delivery of the "automatically alert students below 75% attendance" feature over a 90-day development window:

StageProcessing (Work)WaitingTotal Time
Requirements7 days3 days10 days
Analysis & Design10 days5 days15 days
Coding25 days5 days30 days
Testing12 days8 days20 days
HoD Review & Approval3 days7 days10 days
Deployment3 days2 days5 days
Total60 days30 days90 days
Lead Time = 60 days (Processing) + 30 days (Waiting) = 90 days

Bottleneck identified: the Testing stage carries the single largest wait (8 days), closely followed by HoD Review & Approval (7 days) — together these two stages account for exactly half of all waiting time in the value stream.

10VSM Diagram

Following the reference diagram's convention exactly: each stage is a labelled box, connected by arrows; work time is drawn as a bar rising above the centre line and wait time is drawn as a bar dropping below it.

Reading this diagram Each box is a processing step, linked by arrows in the true order the work moved. Above the centre line, the height of each coloured bar is proportional to the days of active work at that stage; below the line, the height of each rose-coloured bar is proportional to the days spent waiting before the next stage could begin. The two tallest bars below the line — under Testing and HoD Review — visually announce the bottleneck at a glance, without reading a single number.

11Interpretation

  • 67% of the lead time was genuine work; 33% was pure waiting — a very typical split in real software delivery.
  • The relevant Lean question is not "can developers code faster?" but rather: "why is the work waiting between stages, and what would remove that wait?"
  • This is precisely the purpose of Value Stream Mapping: to expose the actual flow of a delivered unit of value and locate where waste — particularly waiting — is concentrated, so effort is directed at the real bottleneck rather than at stages that are already efficient.
14LEAN TOOLS & TECHNIQUES

Five Whys

Definition
Purpose
Problem ID
Symptom vs Root Cause
Five-Why Steps
Example
CAMS Application
Root Cause
Improvement Action
Diagram

1Definition

Five Whys is a root-cause analysis technique, used by Lean teams, that identifies the underlying cause of a problem by repeatedly asking "why?" — moving past the immediate symptom until the deeper, systemic cause becomes visible.

2Purpose

  • To move beyond treating only the visible symptom of a problem.
  • To trace a chain of cause-and-effect back to the one systemic issue that, if fixed, prevents the problem from recurring.
  • To keep the investigation focused on the process, rather than on blaming an individual or a single team.

3Problem Identification

  • Five Whys always begins by stating the problem as a clear, observable symptom — something the team can actually measure or point to.
  • Reference example: "Why is the average lead time so long?"
  • A vague problem statement ("the project feels slow") makes the chain of "whys" unreliable; a measurable one ("lead time exceeds six months") gives each answer something concrete to explain.

4Symptom vs. Root Cause

Symptom (what is observed)Root Cause (what actually produces it)
Feature lead time is too longWork is delivered and reviewed in one large batch instead of small MMFs
"The department head is slow to respond"Senior stakeholders are only shown the software at the final demo, too late to give early input
Key DistinctionA symptom is the visible, reported effect. A root cause is the underlying systemic condition generating that effect. Fixing a symptom without finding the root cause means the same problem resurfaces later, often in a different disguise.

5Five-Why Steps

  1. State the problem as a specific, observable symptom.
  2. Ask "Why does this happen?" and record the immediate, factual answer.
  3. Ask "Why?" again of that answer — treating it as the new symptom to explain.
  4. Repeat the "why" question, typically about five times, until the answers stop describing a specific incident and start describing a systemic process condition.
  5. Confirm the root cause with evidence, then define an improvement action that addresses it directly.
Note"Five" is a guideline, not a strict rule — the chain stops as soon as the answer becomes a genuine process-level cause, whether that takes four questions or six.

6Example (as used by Lean teams)

ProblemThe average lead time for feature requests is too long.
  • Why? Because it is taking over six months for most users' feature requests to make it into the software.
  • Why? Because those feature requests are almost always pushed back to make room on the schedule for last-minute changes.
  • Why? Because before releasing software, the team must review it with senior managers, who almost always ask for basic, foundational changes.
  • Why? Because the senior managers have very specific opinions about how the software should look and function, but the team doesn't hear those opinions until after all the code is built and demoed.
  • Why? Because the senior managers are too busy to talk to the team early in the project, so they only attend the final demo — and send the team back to the drawing board after the software is finished.

7CAMS Application

ProblemThe average lead time for new CAMS features is too long.
  • Why 1: Requests take more than six months to enter the system — because feature requests are pushed back for last-minute changes.
  • Why 2: There are many last-minute changes — because a full review with senior staff happens only right before release.
  • Why 3: Senior review happens only right before release — because the HoD is too busy to engage until the final demo.
  • Why 4: The team only hears feedback after all the code is written — because the whole module is built as one large spec before any review.
  • Why 5 / Root Cause: Work is delivered in one large batch, not small, independently reviewable MMFs.

8Root Cause

Root-Cause Insight The problem is not simply "the department head is slow" or "the team is slow." The deeper process problem is that important stakeholder feedback is arriving too late, because the work is organised in large batches rather than small, independently approvable units. Five Whys pushes attention toward process problems rather than toward blaming individuals — one of its most valuable properties as a diagnostic tool.

9Improvement Action

  • Break the large specification into small MMFs that can each be reviewed and approved independently (§16.2).
  • Involve the HoD / senior stakeholders early — on each small MMF — rather than only at a single, final demo.
  • Introduce a pull system (§16) so approved MMFs move into development immediately, instead of waiting for one large batch to clear review together.

This is exactly the same corrective direction Strategy 1 and Strategy 2 take in the CAMS case study (§18.3–18.4) — Five Whys is what justifies that direction with evidence, rather than adopting it on instinct alone.

10Five-Whys Diagram

Reading this diagram The top box is the observed symptom. Each subsequent box is the answer to "why did the box above it happen?" — the chain moves strictly downward, one cause at a time. The final, highlighted box is the root cause: notice it describes a process characteristic (batching work into one large unit), not a specific person or a one-off event — which is exactly what makes it fixable at the process level.
15LEAN TOOLS & TECHNIQUES

WIP Area Charts

Definition
Meaning of WIP
Purpose
X-axis
Y-axis
MMF Movement
Work Accumulation
Bottleneck ID
Completed Work
CAMS Example
WIP Chart
Interpretation

1Definition

A WIP Area Chart is a diagram that visualises how Minimal Marketable Features (MMFs) flow through the stages of a value stream over time. It is built directly on top of a Value Stream Map (§13) — once a VSM exists for a process, an area chart can be drawn to show how the work moves through those same stages.

2Meaning of WIP

WIP stands for Work In Progress — work that has been started but not yet completed. An MMF counts as WIP the moment it enters the value stream (e.g. is requested or accepted into a stage) and stops counting as WIP the moment it is finished and delivered.

3Purpose

  • To show how much work is currently in progress at any point in time.
  • To show how MMFs move between stages of the value stream.
  • To reveal where work accumulates or stalls — that is, where the bottlenecks are.

4Constructing the Chart — X-axis

  • The x-axis represents date or time (day 0, day 5, day 10 … through the life of the project).

5Constructing the Chart — Y-axis

  • The y-axis represents the number of MMFs currently in progress (0, 3, 6, 9 … up to the largest WIP count reached).

6MMF Movement Across Stages

  • The chart has one line for each stage (box) in the value stream map.
  • As MMFs progress from one stage to the next, a new line and a new shaded band appear beneath the existing one, each representing how many MMFs currently sit at that particular stage.
  • The topmost line always represents total WIP — the sum of every MMF anywhere in the value stream that is not yet done.

7Work Accumulation

  • If the band for a given stage keeps growing wider over time, MMFs are arriving at that stage faster than they are leaving it — work is accumulating there.
  • If total WIP itself keeps rising, it means work is entering the entire system faster than the team can complete it — a Lean warning sign.

8Bottleneck Identification

Note The stage whose band is widest and growing is the bottleneck. The appropriate Lean response is not to hire more developers or push the team to work harder, but to stop starting excessive new work and focus on finishing what has already begun — directly applying the Lean value Deliver as Fast as Possible (§8) at the level of a single stalled stage.

9Completed Work

  • Completed ("done") MMFs are typically removed from the chart, because its purpose is to show current work in progress, not historical throughput.
  • Once an MMF is complete, it is no longer WIP, so it drops out of every band on the chart from that day forward.
  • Different shades or colours are used for each stage's band, so a completed MMF's stripe can be told apart at a glance from the stripes still in progress.

10CAMS Example

The CAMS team's WIP chart is built on top of a small value stream — its five stages, reframed for CAMS, feed directly into the coloured bands of the chart below:

  • The team starts by working with users on nine MMFs (treated as user stories) — this is the initial total WIP.
  • A few days later, at a planning session, the team accepts more work: total WIP rises from 9 to 12 MMFs.
  • Some days after that, 4 of those MMFs progress out of "Collect Feature Requests" and into the "Design Wireframes" stage.

11WIP Chart — Step by Step

Step 1 — Before the project starts (Day 0): there are no MMFs in progress, so the chart begins as a single dot at the origin.

Step 2 — Work enters the first stage: the top line rises from 0, first to 9 MMFs, then a few days later to 12 MMFs, as more work is accepted. The area beneath this line is shaded — this is the number of MMFs sitting in the "Collect Feature Requests" stage.

Step 3 — A second stage appears: once 4 MMFs move into "Design Wireframes," a second line and band are added beneath the first. The top line (total WIP) still reads 12 — it hasn't changed, because no new work entered or left the system, work simply moved from one stage to another.

Step 4 — Full multi-stage chart, completed work removed: as the sprint continues, every stage of the value stream gets its own band, stacked on top of each other. Completed MMFs are dropped from the chart entirely, so the total height at any day equals only the work that is still in progress on that day.

12Interpretation

  • Height of a single band on a given day = number of MMFs currently sitting at that stage.
  • Total height of the stack = total current WIP across the whole value stream.
  • A band that widens steadily while the bands after it stay thin is a visual signature of a bottleneck — MMFs are piling up there because the next stage can't absorb them fast enough.
  • If total WIP keeps climbing over time, the Lean response is to stop starting, start finishing — reduce new work accepted into the value stream until the team's completion rate catches up.
Note The WIP Area Chart and the Value Stream Map are companion tools: the VSM shows where time goes for one feature traced end-to-end, while the WIP chart shows how many features are moving through every stage at once, over the life of the whole project.
16LEAN TOOLS & TECHNIQUES

Pull Systems

Definition A pull system is a way of managing work using queues or buffers to reduce constraints and unevenness in the workflow. Instead of users, managers, or product owners pushing tasks onto a team, requests are placed into a queue that the team pulls from only when it has capacity.

16.1 Why Pull Systems Reduce Waste

  • Pull systems help reduce waiting, excessive WIP, unevenness, overburdening, and workflow bottlenecks.
  • If five developers can comfortably manage five active stories, but a product owner assigns twenty stories simultaneously, most of that work sits partially completed and WIP rises sharply.
  • A queue reverses this — requests wait in the queue, not on the developers' desks, and the team pulls new work only as capacity frees up.
CAMS Example Instead of the product owner assigning all eight planned MMFs at once, the requests sit in a prioritized queue. As soon as the team finishes "Faculty Attendance Marking," it pulls "Low-Attendance Alerts" next — rather than having both, and six others, pushed onto the team simultaneously.

16.2 Small, Pullable Chunks

  • The first step in building an effective pull system is breaking work down into small, pullable chunks.
  • Rather than writing one large specification that must be approved as a single unit, the team breaks it into MMFs — individual stories, each with a small amount of accompanying documentation — that can be approved and pulled independently.
Story 1 → Approval → Development
Story 2 → Approval → Development
Story 3 → Approval → Development
NoteThe advantage is immediate: the first approved MMF can begin development right away. The team is not forced to wait for an entire specification to be finished and approved as one block before any work can start — precisely the batching problem exposed by the Five Whys example in §14.
17SYNTHESIS

How the Concepts Connect

The values and tools covered so far are not independent techniques; they form a single, connected improvement cycle.

  1. Identify waste using the Seven Wastes framework (§5).
  2. Understand the process using Value Stream Mapping (§13).
  3. Find root causes using Five Whys (§14).
  4. Control work in progress using WIP Area Charts (§15).
  5. Improve workflow using Pull Systems (§16).
  6. Deliver faster by reducing cycle time and waiting (§8).
  7. Learn continuously by feeding results back into the process (§6).
One Sentence to Retain Lean Software Development is about maximizing customer value by eliminating waste, improving flow, learning continuously, and delivering valuable software as quickly as possible.
18SYNTHESIS

Case Study: Applying Lean to CAMS

This section consolidates every tool and value covered above into a single, continuous application on CAMS, following the same analytical sequence a Lean team would use in practice.

18.1 The Request

Starting Point The college requests: "Students should be able to view their attendance percentage, and be alerted automatically if it falls below the eligibility threshold."

The delivery flow, before any Lean analysis, follows the familiar stages:

Requirement
→
Design
→
Coding
→
Testing
→
Deployment

18.2 Applying the Seven Wastes to CAMS

WasteObserved in CAMSEffect
Partially Done WorkAttendance, alerts, and reporting modules all started simultaneously; none finishedHigh WIP, no usable feature
Extra ProcessesWeekly progress reports that no stakeholder readsWasted developer hours
Extra FeaturesAn animated attendance-streak badge nobody requestedWasted development effort
Task SwitchingDevelopers rotate between attendance, library, and hostel modulesLoss of focus, cognitive overhead
WaitingTwo days lost waiting for HoD sign-off before deploymentIncreased lead time
MotionRepeated in-person walk-throughs to clarify an undocumented APICommunication delay
DefectsIncorrect attendance percentage for students with mid-term course changes, found post-releaseCostly rework, student complaints

18.3 Strategy 1 — Break Large Work into MMFs

Rather than committing to "build the complete attendance management system" as one undivided unit, the team decomposes it into small, independently deliverable MMFs:

Student Login
Attendance Marking
Percentage Calculation
Low-Attendance Alerts
Correction Requests
HoD Attendance Reports

Fig. 18.1 — CAMS decomposed into independently deliverable MMFs. Each MMF can be reviewed, approved, and deployed independently — the essential precondition for a working pull system.

18.4 Strategy 2 — Introduce a Pull System

Instead of pushing all MMFs to the team at once, requests enter a queue; the team pulls the next MMF only once current work is complete, tested, and delivered (see §16 for the general mechanism).

18.5 Strategy 3 — Reduce Waiting

From the value stream map in §13, waiting accounted for 30 of the 90 total days. Breaking that down by cause:

CauseDays Lost
HoD / department clarification3 days
Design approval5 days
Code review5 days
Testing queue8 days
Stakeholder / user approval7 days
Deployment2 days
  • Possible actions to reduce these delays: obtain stakeholder feedback earlier, review small MMFs rather than large bundled specifications, automate regression testing, reduce unnecessary approval steps, improve communication between the CAMS team and the department office, and establish clear ownership for each approval step.

18.6 Strategy 4 — Build Integrity In

Because attendance data directly affects a student's exam eligibility, calculation defects have real consequences. Rather than discovering percentage-calculation errors during a final testing pass, the team applies continuous testing at every coding step (see §10), stopping to fix a defect the moment it is discovered rather than allowing it to move further into the system.

18.7 Strategy 5 — Reduce Task Switching

Instead of one developer simultaneously supporting the attendance module, the hostel module, and the library module, each developer is assigned focused ownership of a single current MMF — for example, one developer owns "Low-Attendance Alerts" until it is delivered, before picking up the next item from the queue.

18.8 Strategy 6 — Deliver as Fast as Possible

Applying the same cycle-time logic from §8, the team's goal is not to make developers "work faster" in the abstract, but to shrink the gap between a department's request and a working feature reaching students — from roughly 90 days for a bundled release down to approximately 20 days per focused MMF.

18.9 Real-Time Tracking with a Kanban Board

The CAMS team tracks its MMFs on a Kanban-style board, recording when each item enters and leaves a stage:

From this board, the team continuously derives five figures: WIP (how many MMFs are currently unfinished), waiting time (how long an MMF has sat idle), cycle time (time from request to delivery), defects (number detected), and throughput (MMFs completed per period).

19SYNTHESIS

Lean Dashboard and Real-Time Metrics

Lean principles are only useful if they can be observed in practice. Each principle can be converted into a measurable process indicator and tracked on a live dashboard.

Lean PrincipleMetricIllustrative Movement
Eliminate WasteWaiting time30 → 15 days
Deliver FastCycle time30 → 20 days
Empower TeamDecisions made by the team70%
Build Integrity InDefect count18 → 6
See the WholeEnd-to-end lead time90 → 60 days
Reduce WIPActive MMFs12 → 6
Amplify LearningFeedback / improvement actions4 per iteration

These figures are illustrative targets for tracking Lean principles in practice, not prescribed universal benchmarks — actual thresholds should be calibrated to each team's own baseline.

After pull system + smaller MMFs

Fig. 19.1 — CAMS Lean dashboard before and after applying a pull system and smaller MMFs.

Note By Week 4, the CAMS dashboard shows elevated WIP and waiting time. Investigating with Five Whys reveals that many MMFs are stalled awaiting HoD approval — the same batching root cause identified in §14. After introducing a pull system and breaking the large specification into smaller MMFs, Week 6 shows WIP nearly halved, cycle time down, waiting time down, defects down, and completed MMFs more than doubled. The dashboard lets the team observe directly whether a process change actually worked, rather than assuming it did.
20REFERENCE

Glossary of Key Terms

TermMeaning
LeanA mindset focused on eliminating waste and creating value in software development.
Lean ThinkingA business methodology for delivering more value to society and individuals while eliminating waste.
WasteAny activity that does not contribute value to the customer.
MMF (Minimal Marketable Feature)The smallest chunk of a product that customers are willing to prioritize; often a user story or feature request.
Value Stream MappingA technique for visually tracing the flow of a unit of value through a process, to identify waste and waiting.
Five WhysA root-cause analysis technique that repeatedly asks "why?" to reach the underlying cause of a problem.
WIP (Work In Progress)Work that has been started but not yet completed.
Pull SystemA system in which work is pulled by the team based on available capacity, typically using queues or buffers.
Cycle TimeThe time between receiving a feature request and delivering that feature.
Cost of DelayThe economic or practical cost incurred by not delivering a feature sooner.
KaizenContinuous, incremental improvement carried out by the people doing the work.
Just-in-TimeProducing or delivering only what is needed, exactly when it is needed.

Closing Statement Lean does not mean simply making developers work faster. It means improving the entire flow of value — from customer request to delivered software — by removing waste, reducing waiting and work in progress, building quality in from the start, learning continuously, and delivering valuable features as quickly as the system reliably allows.
